vignette:
He is 48, a married man from Oceania, and he has spent most of his adult life working on roofs. He describes roofing as the kind of work that makes sense to him: measure, carry, climb, nail, finish. For years he has liked the physical clarity of it, the way a long day outside leaves his body tired and his mind quieter. Before the assault, he sees himself as reliable, steady, and private. He works hard, comes home dusty and sore, eats with his wife, and does not say much unless there is something worth saying.

The assault happens six years ago, when he is away for a commercial job with a small crew. They are staying in a motel near the site. One night after drinking with the others, he goes back to his room. A man he knows from the job follows later, saying he wants to borrow something. Inside the room, the interaction shifts quickly. He says no, then says it louder, but he is pinned and overpowered. What stays with him afterward is not only fear, but disbelief: the sickening confusion of realizing what is happening while also feeling detached from it, as if his mind has stepped a few feet away from his body. He remembers staring at the motel curtain and the hum of the air conditioner, details that seem sharper than his own voice.

The next morning he goes to work. He tells no one. He cannot bear the idea of saying the words out loud, especially on a crew where men joke roughly and weakness is hunted quickly. He showers until his skin burns. He throws away the clothes he wore that night. When his wife asks why he seems off when he gets home, he says the job was stressful and he is tired. He decides, with a kind of desperate firmness, that if he does not talk about it, he can put it somewhere sealed off.

Instead, the memory begins to move into ordinary life. At work, if someone comes up behind him on a roof and claps a hand on his shoulder, his whole body jerks. He snaps at younger workers for crowding him near ladders or in narrow spaces. He starts insisting on working at the edge of the crew, where he can keep everyone in sight. In enclosed areas-stairwells, supply sheds, motel hallways on out-of-town jobs-his chest tightens and his thoughts scatter. Sometimes the smell of stale beer or cheap detergent pulls him back so fast that for a second he is no longer on a building site but in that room again, frozen and furious.

At night he sleeps lightly. His wife tells him he kicks, shouts, and wakes drenched in sweat. He does not always remember the dream, only the panic and the certainty that something terrible is about to happen. He begins staying up late in the lounge room with the television on low, dozing sitting upright because going to bed feels like walking into an ambush. When his wife reaches for him in sleep, he startles so hard that once he nearly elbows her in the face. After that, a quiet distance grows between them. She thinks at first he is angry with her, or no longer interested in her. He cannot explain that touch has become complicated, that his own body feels unreliable, capable of betraying him with terror when he wants comfort.

He becomes more irritable in ways that embarrass him. Small things set him off: a misplaced tool, traffic, his phone ringing. He drinks more than he used to, not into oblivion but enough to soften the edges for an hour or two. He stops going on overnight jobs whenever he can, even when it costs him money. If a motel stay is unavoidable, he checks the locks repeatedly, wedges a chair under the handle, and sleeps in his work clothes. He chooses rooms near exits. He scans parking lots, notices men's voices, watches hands, doorways, distances.

What unsettles him most is how much of his life is now organized around not remembering. He avoids conversations, movies, and news stories that might touch the subject. He has never reported the assault. He still worries that if he tells people, they will laugh, disbelieve him, or look at him with pity he cannot tolerate. He judges himself harshly for not fighting harder, though he also knows he froze. That argument loops in his head when he is driving, when he is laying shingles, when he catches sight of himself in a window and sees a man who looks solid but does not feel safe.

His wife eventually tells him she feels as though she is living beside someone who is present in body but far away in every other way. That lands heavily. Over several conversations, halting and incomplete, he begins to tell her pieces of what happened. Even now, speaking about that night makes his jaw tighten and his gaze drift to the door. He says he has spent years trying to outwork it, outrun it, outdrink it. But the memory keeps returning-through his sleep, through his temper, through the way he measures every room for threat before he can settle into it. He still climbs roofs each morning, harness on, tools at his waist, doing work he knows well. Yet even high above the ground, in open air, he remains braced for danger that already happened and somehow never fully ended.
